slides.title: No forecast is believed before its backtest
slides.text: How this course works No forecast is believed before its backtest A floor first The best naive forecast is the price of entry. A method that does not beat it is not worth its upkeep. One instrument Every method is scored by the same rolling origins, the same horizon and the same scaled error. Uncertainty is part of the forecast A number without an interval, or an interval nobody checked, is not delivered. AI policy. AI off for the entry and exit checks and for writing the first backtest (Lab 1.4). In the other labs an assistant may explain output, not write the backtest. In the capstone anything goes, defended live.

slides.title: A forecast, a plan and a target are three different numbers
slides.text: Before any model A forecast, a plan and a target are three different numbers Forecast What you expect to happen, with its uncertainty. It can be wrong; it must not be biased on purpose. Plan What you decide to do about it: how much energy to buy, which day to maintain a feeder. Target What someone wants to happen. A target that leaks into a forecast makes both useless. What goes wrong. "Give me one number" hides which of the three is asked for. Ask what will be done with it.

slides.title: "What will demand be?" means something different to each planner
slides.text: Three requests at Shams Power "What will demand be?" means something different to each planner Who asks The decision If the forecast is too low If it is too high Omar, energy purchasing Energy to nominate for each of the next 28 days Buys the gap at about three times the price Resells the surplus at about half price Hamad, network operations The day next week a feeder can be taken out Neighbouring feeders overload A safe day is refused Shahad, load planning Transformer capacity over three years The peak day exceeds capacity Capital is spent early A forecast is worth what the decision it changes is worth. Write the decision down before the first plot.

The highlighted row: 28 days ahead, daily, by region. What goes wrong. The capacity request is not a 28-day model run 39 times. An annual peak is another target.

slides.title: Unequal costs move the answer away from the middle
slides.text: Which number to hand over Unequal costs move the answer away from the middle def target_quantile(cost_under, cost_over): return cost_under / (cost_under + cost_over) target_quantile(2.0, 0.5) # Omar: 0.8 A missing MWh costs Omar two contract prices more; a surplus MWh loses half a price. 80th percentile for purchasing: demand stays under it four days in five 90th percentile for the maintenance request

slides.title: A 28-day forecast from two-day-old data is a 30-step forecast
slides.text: What the desk knows, and when A 28-day forecast from two-day-old data is a 30-step forecast Days ahead Mean change in demand 1 4.3% 2 6.2% 7 8.0% 28 15.0% 30 16.5% Regional meter data reaches the desk two days late. The origin is the last day the model has seen, not the day the forecast is sent. A delay costs most at short horizons: tomorrow becomes step 3, and the change after 2 steps is already 6.2%, against 4.3% after 1.

slides.title: The finer the level, the closer the series is to a household
slides.text: Responsible use The finer the level, the closer the series is to a household A regional total describes a city. A meter describes when a family is home. A feeder that serves a handful of customers sits between the two. Before a fine-grained series leaves the desk, ask the data protection officer whether it can be linked to a person, and so falls under the Personal Data Protection Law. In this course Every series is synthetic and aggregated: regions and feeders, never meters. The capstone uses supplied data, or public data under its stated open-data terms.

slides.title: What do you send back first?
slides.text: Checkpoint What do you send back first? A planner writes: "Send me next month's demand for Al-Sahil by Thursday." Being short costs her four times what being long costs. What does the desk reply with first? The most accurate model's mean forecast for each day One number for the month, the average of the last three years The frame: daily or monthly, which decision, and the 80th percentile The figure in the annual budget, so the two stay consistent

slides.title: Decomposition
slides.text: Session 3 Decomposition Decompose a series with weekly and annual seasons Compute the strength of trend and of seasonality Read the remainder for holidays, outages and breaks 03

slides.title: Split the series into parts you can name, and one you cannot
slides.text: Decomposition Split the series into parts you can name, and one you cannot Trend the slow level: growth, new feeders + Weekly season Friday and Saturday + Annual season the summer + Remainder everything else On the log scale. Summer swings are larger in MWh when the level is higher, so the parts multiply. Taking the logarithm turns the product into this sum.

slides.title: A decomposition with two seasonal periods, robust to odd days
slides.text: The tool A decomposition with two seasonal periods, robust to odd days from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import MSTL res = MSTL(np.log(y), periods=(7, 365), stl_kwargs={"robust": True}).fit() res.trend res.seasonal["seasonal_7"] res.seasonal["seasonal_365"] res.resid Each season is smoothed over its own cycles and may change slowly over the years. Robust fitting gives an odd day little weight, so an outage stays in the remainder and does not bend the season. The four parts add up to the log of demand exactly. Check it.

slides.title: Strength compares a component with the noise around it
slides.text: A number per part Strength compares a component with the noise around it def strength(component, remainder): ratio = remainder.var() / ( component + remainder).var() return max(0.0, 1 - ratio) Al-Rimal, 2017 to 2025 Strength Annual season 0.96 Trend 0.50 Weekly season 0.16 Read it as. Near 1: the component dominates the remainder. Near 0: it is lost in it.

slides.title: The remainder is the to-do list of the next model
slides.text: Read what is left The remainder is the to-do list of the next model -13% mean remainder on the 54 main Eid days of nine years 2 of 12 largest remainders are Eid days; most are weather swings -0.35 log remainder on 14 March 2023, the outage What goes wrong. Expecting holidays to top the list. In a hot region a week that is warmer or cooler than normal moves demand more than Eid does.

slides.title: Al-Mina grew 52% in two years: a step, not a trend
slides.text: Structural breaks Al-Mina grew 52% in two years: a step, not a trend On 1 July 2022 six industrial feeders joined the region. A decomposition smooths the step into a steep trend. A model trained across the step reads it as fast growth, or averages two levels. Options Train after the break. Or tell the model: a step regressor, or forecast the new feeders apart. How you find out The yearly means, then a question to network operations.

slides.text: Checkpoint What does this remainder tell you? You decompose a region's log demand with weekly and annual periods. slides.title: The benchmark floor
slides.text: Session 4 The benchmark floor Write naive and seasonal-naive forecasts Run a rolling-origin backtest over 28-day horizons Report scaled errors by horizon and name the floor 04

slides.title: Before any model, find out how good "no model" is
slides.text: The benchmark floor Before any model, find out how good "no model" is It costs nothing No fitting, no tuning, no upkeep. It cannot break in production. It is often good On strongly seasonal series, repeating the right past period is hard to beat. It sets the price Every later method reports its distance to the floor, not its own error alone. What goes wrong. "Our model has a 4% error" says nothing until you know that repeating last year gives 5%, or 3%.

slides.title: Naive repeats the last day; seasonal naive repeats the last cycle
slides.text: Three ways to repeat the past Naive repeats the last day; seasonal naive repeats the last cycle def naive(train, h): return np.repeat(train.iloc[-1], h) def seasonal_naive(train, h, m): last = train.to_numpy()[-m:] return np.resize(last, h) Method Next Friday equals Naive the last day seen Seasonal naive, m = 7 last Friday Seasonal naive, m = 364 the Friday 52 weeks ago 364, not 365. Fifty-two whole weeks keep a Friday on a Friday.

slides.title: Move the origin through the last year and forecast 28 days each time
slides.text: The instrument Move the origin through the last year and forecast 28 days each time 3,3414,1865,0325,878origin 18 Jun 2025 One fold. Solid: what happened. Dashed coral: last week repeated. Teal: the same weekdays a year earlier. The origin is the last day the forecaster has seen. 13 origins, 28 days apart: every day of 2025 is tested exactly once. Each fold trains on the 1,096 days before its origin. Nothing after the origin may reach the forecast.

slides.title: A scaled error lets a region and a feeder share one table
slides.text: The measure A scaled error lets a region and a feeder share one table def scaled_error(actual, forecast, train, m=7): v = train.to_numpy() scale = np.mean(np.abs(v[m:] - v[:-m])) err = np.mean(np.abs(actual - forecast)) return err / scale The numerator: mean absolute error on the test days. The denominator: the error of "last week" inside the training data, one week ahead. No unit. Below 1 beats that in-sample error. Above 1 at 28 days is normal: the yardstick is one week ahead.

slides.title: The floor is "the same weekday last year", at 1.06
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · Al-Rimal, 13 origins, 364 test days The floor is "the same weekday last year", at 1.06 Method Scaled error Week 1 Week 2 Week 3 Week 4 Naive (last day) 1.64 1.09 1.87 1.55 2.07 Last week (m = 7) 1.62 1.18 1.77 1.46 2.05 Same weekday last year (m = 364) 1.06 0.92 0.96 1.08 1.28 Report by horizon. One average hides that "last week" is close in week 1 and twice as bad in week 4.

slides.title: On Eid days the floor's error doubles
slides.text: Know your floor's weak days On Eid days the floor's error doubles 2.17 scaled error of the floor on the 11 Eid days of 2025 1.03 on the other 353 days Last year's Eid was about 11 days later: the floor puts the dip on the wrong days. Eleven days are 3% of the year, so the overall score barely moves. They are the days the purchasing lead remembers.

slides.title: Which backtest is a fair floor?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which backtest is a fair floor? A colleague reports a floor for a 28-day daily forecast: seasonal naive with m = 7, tested on the 28 days after one origin in January, error 0.28 after scaling. What is the main weakness? The scale should come from the test days, not the training days One origin in a calm month says little about the other eleven A seasonal naive forecast is too simple to count as a floor The horizon should be shortened to 7 days to match m = 7

slides.text: Review · Day 1 What does the scaled error compare? A method scores 1.3 on a region in the course's backtest. The floor scores 1.06. A colleague says: "Above 1, so it is worse than a naive forecast and useless." What is the right reading? slides.title: A weighted average that forgets the past at a rate you choose
slides.text: Simple exponential smoothing A weighted average that forgets the past at a rate you choose def ses_level(values, alpha): level = values[0] for x in values[1:]: level = alpha * x + (1 - alpha) * level return level # the forecast, for every h The value k days back has the weight alpha * (1 - alpha) ** k. alpha near 0: a long memory, a smooth level. alpha = 1: the level is the last value. That is the naive forecast. The forecast is flat: the same level for every day ahead.

slides.title: On daily demand the best alpha is at the top of the grid
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · step 1 On daily demand the best alpha is at the top of the grid alpha One-step error, MWh 0.1 251.0 0.3 187.5 0.5 170.7 0.7 161.4 0.9 157.3 1.0 156.3 Why Demand moves in weather spells that last days. Yesterday is a better guide to today than any average of the past. What it means Smoothing has nothing to smooth here. The model is close to "tomorrow equals today".

slides.title: Level plus an optional trend plus an optional season
slides.text: The ETS family Level plus an optional trend plus an optional season Error Additive or multiplicative. It decides the shape of the intervals. Trend None, additive, or damped: a slope that fades with the horizon. Season None, additive or multiplicative, with one period: here 7 days. from statsforecast.models import AutoETS U.sf(AutoETS(season_length=7, model="ANA"), train, h) # additive error, no trend, additive season

slides.title: Difference until the level stops wandering, then model the memory
slides.text: ARIMA Difference until the level stops wandering, then model the memory I · differencing Work on changes, not levels. A seasonal difference subtracts the same weekday of last week. AR · autoregression Today depends on the last few days, each with a coefficient. MA · moving average Today depends on the last few forecast errors. Written as. ARIMA(p, d, q)(P, D, Q) with a period m: the first bracket for day-to-day memory, the second for week-to-week.

slides.title: The autocorrelation says whether differencing has done its work
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · step 1 The autocorrelation says whether differencing has done its work Lag in days 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 Demand 0.98 0.97 0.96 0.95 0.94 0.94 0.94 After a seasonal difference 0.83 0.59 0.40 0.24 0.08 -0.09 -0.21 Before. Correlations that stay near 1: the level wanders. Nothing to model yet. After. Memory that dies out in five days, and a dip at lag 7: a short AR part and a seasonal MA term.

slides.title: The weekly ARIMA has the same blindness as the weekly ETS
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · step 2 The weekly ARIMA has the same blindness as the weekly ETS from statsforecast.models import ARIMA def weekly_arima(): return ARIMA(order=(1, 0, 1), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1), season_length=7) U.sf(weekly_arima(), train, h) 1.62 scaled error, against 1.59 for the weekly ETS and 1.06 for the floor Two families, one miss. Neither can see the summer through a period of 7.

slides.title: If the residuals still hold a pattern, the model has not finished
slides.text: Diagnostics If the residuals still hold a pattern, the model has not finished Residuals are the one-step errors inside the training data. A finished model leaves noise: no autocorrelation. The Ljung-Box test asks whether the first 14 autocorrelations together are larger than noise gives. A small p-value: a pattern is left, and the model's intervals, which assume noise, cannot be trusted. 0.0001 p-value of the weekly ARIMA: not noise acorr_ljungbox(residuals, lags=[14], model_df=3)["lb_pvalue"]

slides.title: Two pairs of annual waves give ARIMA the summer
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · step 4 Two pairs of annual waves give ARIMA the summer def fourier(dates, K=2): t = days_since_2017(dates) return DataFrame({ f"{f}{k}": getattr(np, f)( 2 * np.pi * k * t / 365.25) for k in (1, 2) for f in ("sin", "cos")}) U.sf(weekly_arima(), train, h, fourier(train.index), fourier(future)) 0.83 scaled error: 22% under the floor 0.62 Ljung-Box p-value: the residuals pass

slides.title: Pinball loss charges a quantile unequally for its two kinds of miss
slides.text: The score for a quantile Pinball loss charges a quantile unequally for its two kinds of miss def pinball(y, q, tau): return np.mean(np.where( y >= q, tau * (y - q), # too low (1 - tau) * (q - y))) # too high pinball([10], [8], 0.9) # 1.8 pinball([10], [12], 0.9) # 0.2 A 0.9 quantile pays nine times as much for being too low as for being too high. That is the cost structure of Day 1's planner: the quantile is the cost ratio. At 0.5 it is half the absolute error. Lower is better. Averaged over several quantiles it scores the whole forecast distribution.

slides.title: Two simple ways to make them add up
slides.text: Reconciliation Two simple ways to make them add up Bottom-up Keep the feeder forecasts. The region is their sum. Throws away the regional model, with its temperature and calendar. Top-down Keep the regional forecast. Split it by each feeder's share of the feeder forecasts, day by day. Throws away the level of every feeder model, and keeps its share. share = feeders_fc.div(feeders_fc.sum(axis=1), axis=0) top_down = share.mul(region_fc, axis=0)

slides.title: Least squares: move every forecast as little as possible
slides.text: Use both levels Least squares: move every forecast as little as possible Find the coherent set of forecasts closest to the base forecasts, in squared distance. For one region with n feeders the answer is closed: every feeder takes an equal part of the gap. With 37 feeders the total lands almost on the regional forecast. n = feeders_fc.shape[1] gap = region_fc - feeders_fc.sum(axis=1) least_sq = feeders_fc.add(gap / (n + 1), axis=0) The equal share is the weakness. A feeder of 30 MWh and one of 175 MWh receive the same correction in MWh.

slides.title: A score far below every honest result is a finding to explain
slides.text: A backtest arrives for review A score far below every honest result is a finding to explain 1.06 the floor, Al-Rimal, 13 origins over 2025 0.77 the regression of Lab 2.3 with weather and calendar 0.24 the backtest you are asked to review The reviewer's first question. What does this forecast know on the origin day, and how does it know it?

slides.title: Three doors through which the future reaches a forecast
slides.text: Leakage across time Three doors through which the future reaches a forecast 1 · A feature A column computed from the series itself that reaches past the origin: a centred average, a lag shorter than the horizon. 2 · A regressor An outside variable used with values that were not known on the origin day: measured weather, revised figures. 3 · A choice A model, setting or window picked because it scored best on the test folds. No column leaks; the decision does.

slides.title: A centred average contains the days being forecast
slides.text: Lab 4.1 · step 2 A centred average contains the days being forecast X["smooth"] = data.demand.rolling(7, center=True, min_periods=1).mean().reindex(dates) # t-3 to t+3 X["smooth"] = data.demand.rolling(7).mean().shift(28).reindex(dates) # ends 28 days before t 0.24 → 0.41 scaled error before and after the fix The rule. A feature built from the target must end at least one horizon before the day it describes: here 28 days.

slides.title: The measured temperature of the test days was never available
slides.text: Lab 4.1 · step 3 The measured temperature of the test days was never available temp = data.temp_c.reindex(dates) # measured: fine up to the origin temp = temp.where(dates <= origin, U.temp_known(RID, origin, dates)) # after it: what was known X["cdd"] = (temp - 22).clip(lower=0) 0.41 → 0.71 scaled error before and after the fix The rule. For every outside variable ask what its value was on the origin day, not what it turned out to be.

slides.title: Methods that err in different directions cancel part of each other's error
slides.text: Combining forecasts Methods that err in different directions cancel part of each other's error The error of an average is never above the average of the errors. The gain is larger the less the methods' errors move together. Three models from one family, fed the same inputs, cancel little. The three in Lab 4.3 Decompose then ETS: seasons only. ARIMA with annual Fourier terms: seasons and recent errors. Regression: temperature and calendar. Three views of one series. The simple average has no settings. Nothing to tune means nothing to tune on the test window.

slides.title: A forecast note has six parts, and the planner reads the first three
slides.text: Lab 4.4 · step 3 A forecast note has six parts, and the planner reads the first three 1 · Decision What is forecast, for which days, for which decision. 2 · Forecast The range of the median, and the quantile the reader acts on. 3 · Uncertainty What the bands mean and how often they held. 4 · Evidence The backtest score against the floor, in one sentence. 5 · Limits When not to use it, and when to ask for a rerun. 6 · Source Data up to which day, the method in one line, who signs.

slides.title: Say when the forecast should not be used
slides.text: The part most notes leave out Say when the forecast should not be used Outside its scope: not for one feeder, not for hours within the day, not beyond 28 days. When its assumptions break: a declared heat wave or dust storm; a holiday date that moves. What it never forecasts: outages. Why it protects the reader Shahad Al-Tamimi asked for the peak day three years ahead. A 28-day forecast stretched to answer her would carry these bands into a question they were never measured on. Each limit names a situation and an action: do not use, or ask for a rerun.
